Chapter 7: The Role of Ideology and the Destruction of Reality.
Have you ever had that feeling—when the world you thought you knew just... slips away? The facts you used to trust start to wobble. Suddenly, the stories all around you just don’t line up with what you’ve experienced yourself.
Under a totalitarian regime, that confusion isn’t just a side effect. It’s actually the point. The people in power use ideology almost like a tool, twisting reality until the impossible starts to feel true.
Picture someone listening to a speech that turns everything upside down. Yesterday’s friends? Now, they’re called enemies. Words you thought you understood begin to change meaning from one day to the next. At first, you might brush it off—call it propaganda, or just stick to what you know is real.
But as the pressure builds, it gets harder. Questioning the official story suddenly feels risky. And the rewards for just going along? Well, they start to look more and more appealing.
Here’s something important: ideology, in this setting, isn’t just a list of beliefs. It’s a whole system for organizing the world—deciding what’s true, and what’s not even allowed to be noticed. The regime’s version of reality becomes the only one that counts. If you don’t buy in, you’re not just out of step... you’re pushed aside, or worse.
What’s really unsettling is how this ideology seeps into everyday life. Kids pick up new versions of history at school. Neighbors start repeating slogans they don’t really understand. Even your private thoughts can get twisted, shaped by the urge to fit in.
Soon, it’s tough to tell where real belief ends and just playing along begins.
Of course, some people try to resist. They hold tight to their memories, or cling to private truths. But the pressure never lets up. And standing out comes with real risks. Eventually, the regime’s reality is the only safe place to hide.
The destruction of reality isn’t just about censorship or spreading lies. It’s about remaking the world, from the inside out.
Most of the time, people barely notice the change while it’s happening. It’s easy to tell yourself you can keep your own truth—even as you nod along with the official line. But the longer things go on, the harder it gets to tell what you really know, apart from what you’ve been told.
The process is slow, almost invisible, but the impact? It’s life-changing.
